blocks.content: 1. Introduction
Your fridge does not call you every time the temperature ticks up half a degree. It only alerts you, with a beep or a light, when the temperature crosses a point where your food is actually at risk.

That is the entire idea behind alerting. You already have metrics flowing in from every service. Alerting is the layer that watches those metrics and decides when a human actually needs to be interrupted.
An alert is a rule that fires when a metric crosses a threshold for some duration, and then notifies a human or triggers automation.

Monitoring, in the broad sense, is collecting and visualizing the numbers. Alerting is the narrower, sharper practice built on top of it: deciding which of those numbers are worth waking someone up for.
1.1 What An Alert Actually Is

Strip away the tooling and an alert rule is just three things: a metric, a threshold, and a duration. CPU usage above 90 percent for 10 minutes. Error rate above 5 percent for 5 minutes. Queue depth above 10,000 for 2 minutes.

The duration matters as much as the threshold. Without it, a single one second spike would page someone every few minutes, for a system that is actually fine. Requiring the condition to hold for a stretch of time filters out normal noise and only fires for something sustained.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396528029-496630004.png
blocks.alt: A metric climbing past a threshold line and triggering an alert after it stays breached

blocks.content: 1.2 Where Alerting Fits On Top Of Metrics
blocks.text: 1.2 Where Alerting Fits On Top Of Metrics

blocks.content: You cannot alert on what you do not measure. Alerting sits directly on top of the metrics pipeline: something scrapes or receives the numbers, stores them, and a separate rules engine evaluates conditions against that stored data continuously.
Get the metrics wrong, missing labels, wrong aggregation, sampling gaps, and every alert built on top inherits that weakness. Good alerting starts with metrics you actually trust.

blocks.title: Not a replacement for dashboards
blocks.content: Alerting and dashboards serve different jobs. A dashboard is for a human actively looking, exploring, debugging. An alert is for the moment nobody is looking, and something needs their attention anyway.
2. Symptom Based Alerting Versus Cause Based Alerting
blocks.text: 2. Symptom Based Alerting Versus Cause Based Alerting

blocks.content: This is the single most important decision in designing an alerting strategy, and it is the one that separates teams that trust their alerts from teams that have learned to ignore them.
2.1 Symptom Based Alerting
A symptom is something the user actually experiences: requests are failing, pages are loading slowly, checkout is timing out. Symptom based alerting fires on these user facing effects directly.
["Elevated error rate on customer facing endpoints","Elevated p99 latency on the checkout flow","A drop in successful login rate","Requests per second falling to zero on a critical path"]
items: Elevated error rate on customer facing endpoints
Elevated p99 latency on the checkout flow
A drop in successful login rate
Requests per second falling to zero on a critical path

blocks.content: Notice what these have in common. Every single one means a real user is having a bad time right now. That is exactly why they deserve to interrupt a human.
2.2 Cause Based Alerting

A cause is an internal signal that might, eventually, lead to a symptom. Disk usage climbing. A garbage collection pause getting longer. One replica out of twenty running a slightly older version. Thread pool utilization creeping up.

The problem is that most internal signals never actually turn into a user facing problem. Disk usage climbing slowly might get resolved by a scheduled cleanup job before it matters. A single replica lagging might get rebalanced automatically. Alerting on every one of these treats every internal wobble as an emergency, when most of them are not.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396528030-886267677.png
blocks.alt: User facing error rate feeding a symptom alert while noisy internal signals feed cause based alerts

blocks.content: 2.3 Why Symptoms Win

The practical rule is: alert on symptoms, page a human for those. Track causes too, but mostly as dashboard data and lower priority signals a human looks at during business hours, or as inputs the on call engineer checks once a symptom alert has already fired and they are digging for the root cause.

blocks.title: Causes still matter, just not as pages
blocks.content: You still want cause level metrics around: they are exactly what an engineer looks at after a symptom based page fires, to figure out why. The distinction is not "measure causes or not", it is "page on causes or not".
Alert on what the user experiences, not on every internal signal that theoretically could affect them.
3. Alert Fatigue

Alert fatigue is the central danger in any alerting system, and it is almost always self inflicted. It happens gradually, one reasonable sounding alert at a time, until the system that was supposed to protect you starts working against you.
3.1 How Alert Fatigue Forms

It starts innocently. Someone adds an alert for a metric they are worried about. Then another. Then one that fires on a known flaky check, and nobody removes it because it is technically correct sometimes. A few months in, the on call engineer is getting paged five, ten, twenty times a night, and most of those pages resolve themselves or turn out to be nothing.

["Alerts that fire for conditions with no real user impact","Alerts that are frequently false positives, or flap on and off repeatedly","Duplicate alerts for the same underlying problem, one per affected pod or server","Alerts nobody has looked at or tuned since the day they were created"]
items: Alerts that fire for conditions with no real user impact
Alerts that are frequently false positives, or flap on and off repeatedly
Duplicate alerts for the same underlying problem, one per affected pod or server
Alerts nobody has looked at or tuned since the day they were created

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396528030-409958000.png
blocks.alt: Multiple alerts flooding an on call phone, leading the engineer to mute pages and miss a real incident

blocks.content: 3.2 The Real Cost: Missed Incidents

Here is the part that makes alert fatigue dangerous rather than just annoying. Once an engineer has been paged at 3am five nights in a row for nothing, they stop trusting the pager. They start snoozing notifications, or acknowledging without really reading them, or muting the whole channel on a bad week.
And then the one night a real, user impacting incident happens, it looks exactly like the ninety nine false alarms that came before it. Nobody reacts in time, because the system trained them not to.

blocks.title: The boy who cried wolf, in production
blocks.text: A team wired up an alert for every pod restart, even routine ones from normal deployments. Within a month the on call rotation was getting paged 40 times a day. Engineers started acknowledging pages without reading them, just to make the noise stop. When a real memory leak started crashing pods every few minutes during a traffic spike, the page looked identical to the routine noise, and it sat unacknowledged for twenty minutes before anyone actually looked.

blocks.content: 4. Every Alert Should Be Actionable

The single best filter for whether something deserves to be a page is simple: if this fires right now, is there something a human can and should do about it immediately? If the answer is no, it should not interrupt anyone.
4.1 The Actionability Test

Before adding any new page, ask what the on call engineer is actually supposed to do when it fires. If the honest answer is "nothing, it will resolve itself" or "just note it and move on", that alert does not belong on the pager.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396528031-197579947.png
blocks.alt: An elevated error rate alert that pages on call next to a low priority disk metric routed to a dashboard instead

blocks.content: {"headers":["Actionable, should page","Not actionable, should not page"],"rows":[["Error rate breaching a threshold that affects real users right now","Disk usage at 40 percent with weeks of runway left"],["A critical service returning zero successful responses","A single log line matching a rare but harmless pattern"],["Latency degraded badly enough that customers are affected now","A metric that self corrects within its own normal cycle"]]}
4.2 Downgrade Instead Of Page

Non actionable signals are not useless, they just do not belong on a pager. Route them somewhere quieter: a dashboard panel someone checks during business hours, a low priority ticket, or a weekly digest email. The goal is not to throw away the signal, it is to stop treating every signal as an emergency.

blocks.title: A useful gut check
blocks.content: If an alert has fired the same way ten times in a row and nobody has changed anything about the system in response, that alert is not actionable. Either fix what it is measuring, delete it, or downgrade it off the pager.
5. Alert Routing And Escalation
Deciding an alert should page someone is only half the job. The other half is making sure it pages the right someone, and that it does not just sit there forever if that person misses it.
5.1 Routing To The Right On Call Engineer
blocks.text: 5.1 Routing To The Right On Call Engineer

blocks.content: A large system has many teams, and a payments error has nothing to do with the search team. Routing rules match an alert firing labels, like service or team, to the specific on call rotation responsible for that piece of the system.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396528031-674522038.png
blocks.alt: An alert firing and a router sending it to the on call engineer for the correct owning team

blocks.content: Get routing wrong and you get one of two bad outcomes: alerts that go to nobody because they were misrouted, or alerts that go to everyone because nobody set up specific routing at all.
5.2 Escalation Policies

People miss pages. Phones die, someone is asleep, someone is already handling a different incident. An escalation policy defines what happens if the primary on call does not acknowledge within some window, usually by paging a secondary on call, then a team lead, then possibly a wider incident channel.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396528032-275772792.png
blocks.alt: An unacknowledged alert escalating from primary on call to secondary on call to a team lead

blocks.title: Set the escalation window deliberately
blocks.content: Too short and you page a second person before the first one even had a chance to look. Too long and a real incident sits unattended for half an hour. Somewhere around 10 to 15 minutes is a common starting point, then tune it against how your team actually responds.
5.3 Avoiding The Firehose

Do not let every alert in the system route to one poor engineer regardless of what it is about. Split ownership by service or team, use grouping so twenty related alerts become one page instead of twenty, and make sure the routing rules are actually tested, not just written once and forgotten.
6. Alerting And SLOs
Once a team has service level objectives defined, the sharpest alerting strategy is often not a raw metric threshold at all, it is the rate at which the error budget is burning.
6.1 Error Budget Burn Rate Alerts

If your SLO allows 0.1 percent of requests to fail over a month, that failure allowance is your error budget. A burn rate alert fires when you are consuming that budget faster than the month can sustain, for example if the current failure rate would exhaust the entire monthly budget in a few hours.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396528032-239938479.png
blocks.alt: An error budget draining quickly and triggering a burn rate alert before the whole budget is gone

blocks.content: This approach is naturally symptom based and naturally resistant to noise, since a single blip barely dents a monthly budget, but a sustained problem burns through it fast and pages appropriately. The full mechanics of SLOs, error budgets, and burn rate math live in the dedicated SLO topic, this section only covers where alerting plugs into that model.
7. Real Tooling
The concepts above are tool agnostic, but it helps to know what actually implements them in a typical production stack.
7.1 Prometheus Alertmanager

Prometheus evaluates alert rules against the metrics it has scraped, and when a rule fires, it hands the alert off to Alertmanager. Alertmanager is specifically the routing layer: it groups related alerts together, deduplicates repeats of the same underlying problem, silences known maintenance windows, and routes each alert to the right notification channel.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396528672-40614896.png
blocks.alt: Three related pod alerts arriving at Alertmanager and being grouped into a single notification

blocks.content: 7.2 PagerDuty And Opsgenie

PagerDuty and Opsgenie sit one layer above Alertmanager. They own the on call schedule itself, who is primary this week, who is secondary, and the escalation policy, and they are the ones that actually ring a phone, send a push notification, or place a phone call.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396528674-87844149.png
blocks.alt: A weekly on call rotation feeding into who is actively paged today

blocks.content: 7.3 Grafana Alerting

Grafana Alerting lets you define alert rules directly against the same dashboards you already use to visualize metrics, and it can send notifications through many of the same channels, including PagerDuty and Opsgenie. Many teams use it as a lighter weight alternative to a separate Alertmanager setup, especially when Grafana is already the primary place engineers look at metrics.
8. Worked Example: A Complete Alert Rule
blocks.text: 8. Worked Example: A Complete Alert Rule

blocks.content: Put the pieces together with one concrete rule: page the on call engineer if the error rate exceeds 5 percent for 5 minutes, and escalate if nobody acknowledges within 10 minutes.
8.1 The Prometheus Alert Rule
The rule itself lives in Prometheus, expressed against the error rate metric already being scraped from the service.

groups:
  - name: checkout-service-alerts
    rules:
      - alert: HighErrorRate
        expr: |
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout", status=~"5.."}[5m]))
          /
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout"}[5m]))
          > 0.05
        for: 5m
        labels:
          severity: page
          team: checkout
        annotations:
          summary: "Checkout error rate above 5 percent"
          description: "Error rate has been above 5 percent for 5 minutes on the checkout service."

code.content:
groups:
  - name: checkout-service-alerts
    rules:
      - alert: HighErrorRate
        expr: |
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout", status=~"5.."}[5m]))
          /
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout"}[5m]))
          > 0.05
        for: 5m
        labels:
          severity: page
          team: checkout
        annotations:
          summary: "Checkout error rate above 5 percent"
          description: "Error rate has been above 5 percent for 5 minutes on the checkout service."

codes.yaml:
groups:
  - name: checkout-service-alerts
    rules:
      - alert: HighErrorRate
        expr: |
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout", status=~"5.."}[5m]))
          /
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout"}[5m]))
          > 0.05
        for: 5m
        labels:
          severity: page
          team: checkout
        annotations:
          summary: "Checkout error rate above 5 percent"
          description: "Error rate has been above 5 percent for 5 minutes on the checkout service."

blocks.content: The expr computes the ratio of 5xx responses to total requests over a 5 minute window. The for: 5m clause is what stops a brief 10 second spike from paging anyone, the condition has to hold for the full 5 minutes before it counts as firing.
8.2 Alertmanager Routing Config
Once Prometheus fires the alert, Alertmanager decides where it goes based on its labels.

route:
  receiver: default-slack
  group_by: ["alertname", "team"]
  group_wait: 30s
  group_interval: 5m
  repeat_interval: 4h
  routes:
    - match:
        severity: page
        team: checkout
      receiver: checkout-pagerduty
      continue: false

receivers:
  - name: checkout-pagerduty
    pagerduty_configs:
      - service_key: "<checkout-team-pagerduty-integration-key>"
        severity: critical

blocks.content: The match on severity: page and team: checkout sends this specific alert to the checkout team PagerDuty integration, while everything else falls through to the default Slack receiver. group_by keeps repeated firings of the same alert from paging repeatedly during the same incident.
8.3 What Happens End To End
Walk through the full path once the error rate actually crosses 5 percent and stays there.

["Prometheus evaluates HighErrorRate every scrape interval and sees the condition has now held for 5 minutes","The alert fires and is sent to Alertmanager with its labels attached","Alertmanager matches the team: checkout and severity: page labels and routes it to the checkout PagerDuty integration","PagerDuty pages the primary on call engineer for the checkout rotation","If nobody acknowledges within 10 minutes, PagerDuty escalates to the secondary on call engineer"]

The alert fires and is sent to Alertmanager with its labels attached
Alertmanager matches the team: checkout and severity: page labels and routes it to the checkout PagerDuty integration

If nobody acknowledges within 10 minutes, PagerDuty escalates to the secondary on call engineer

blocks.alt: The error rate crossing 5 percent, firing an alert, paging on call through PagerDuty, and escalating after 10 minutes unacknowledged

blocks.title: Where the two configs meet
blocks.content: The labels in the Prometheus rule, severity and team, are exactly what the Alertmanager route matches against. Get the labels wrong or inconsistent between the two files and the alert either goes nowhere or goes to the wrong team.
9. Alerting In System Design Interviews
Alerting rarely gets asked about directly as its own question, but it shows up naturally the moment an interview turns to reliability, on call, or operating a system at scale.

What separates a strong answer from a weak one is almost never knowledge of a specific tool. It is whether the candidate instinctively reaches for symptom based alerting instead of listing every internal metric they can think of and proposing an alert for each one.

["Say you would alert on user facing symptoms first: error rate, latency, availability, not every internal signal","Mention the actionability test, if nobody can act on it right now, it should not page","Bring up alert fatigue unprompted as the reason symptom based alerting matters","Mention routing and escalation briefly, so an alert reaches the right person and does not get lost if missed","If SLOs come up, connect alerting to error budget burn rate rather than a flat threshold"]
items: Say you would alert on user facing symptoms first: error rate, latency, availability, not every internal signal
Mention the actionability test, if nobody can act on it right now, it should not page
Bring up alert fatigue unprompted as the reason symptom based alerting matters
Mention routing and escalation briefly, so an alert reaches the right person and does not get lost if missed
If SLOs come up, connect alerting to error budget burn rate rather than a flat threshold

blocks.title: A strong signal of real experience
blocks.content: Anyone can say "add monitoring". Explaining specifically why you would alert on symptoms rather than every possible cause, and why that avoids alert fatigue, tells an interviewer you have actually carried a pager before.
